newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's top parties want truth commission.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's top parties want truth commission.

text.p: Leaders of Nicaragua's top political parties on Tuesday called for the formation of a truth commission to investigate human rights abuses committed during Nicaragua's civil war.

Unlike neighbouring El Salvador, Nicaragua never formed a truth commission after its civil war ended in 1990. The unresolved issue of clandestine graves containing bodies of victims killed by both sides has become an issue in its October 20 presidential election.

Presidential candidate Arnoldo Aleman, who is leading in the polls, told reporters that if he wins the election, his government will form a truth commission to investigate human rights abuses during the 1979-1990 Sandinista revolutionary government.
"The truth commission won't be to judge people and put them in prison, but to let the families of the victims know what happened to their children and husbands," Aleman said.

Alvaro Fiallos, Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega's campaign chief, responded that a Sandinista government would support such a truth commission, as long as it investigated crimes committed by both sides during the war.

At the end of the civil war, Nicaragua passed an amnesty law for human rights abuses committed by the Sandinista army and the U.S.-backed Contra rebels, who fought an eight-year war in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead.

The government has not conducted a serious investigation into human rights abuses in the name of national reconciliation, said Lino Hernandez, president of the pro-Contra Permanent Commission for Human Rights.
"The attitude in Nicaragua has been indifference," said Hernandez, whose group has collected evidence that 1,200 people disappeared between 1979 and 1990, most by the Sandinista army.
Vilma Nunez of the pro-Sandinista Nicaraguan Centre for Human Rights said her group had a list of 862 people who disappeared after being detained by the Contras.
